channel.title: Koichi Osamura: Stories
channel.description: A closer look at my published (or not) research, told through data visualization, using Claude to help draft the interactive plots.

item.title: Brazil’s 2026 runoff, by polling station
item.description:
Back to Stories

Introduction

I’ve never liked those election maps that paint an entire state one colour or the other after the runoff. A few days ago, I saw a comment on some social network (I don’t remember which) saying that “land doesn’t vote”. I found the line brilliant, and it makes total sense. Anyone who knows Brazil, and isn’t trying to push a biased picture of one region or another, knows that much of the country isn’t actually inhabited. We do have (yes!) forests and other nature reserves, but also huge private estates and areas unfit for housing: just think of the massive mountain wall, the Serra do Mar, that separates the city of São Paulo from the coast at Santos. But let’s leave that conversation for another day.

NoteSource

All data were obtained from the Brazilian electoral court (TSE) open data website.

Each dot is one polling station: all the sections (seções) that vote in the same building are combined. The colour shows which candidate led there and by how much, and the dot’s size shows how many valid votes were cast. Zoom in to see individual neighbourhoods, and hover over (or tap) a dot for the details.

The data were prepared in R with the good old tidyverse, sf and geobr packages, and the map is drawn with MapLibre GL JS on an OpenFreeMap base map built from OpenStreetMap data.

Where do we vote, and who do we vote for?

With this idea that “land doesn’t vote” in mind, I decided to put my free time (cough cough) to good use and play around with data from the TSE, Brazil’s electoral court. I created an interactive map with the results of the presidential runoff. It shows the number and share of votes that Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro received at each polling place (when an address has more than one voting section, the votes are added up and the share is calculated on the address total). Right away, the map shows that Brazilians are indeed concentrated in specific areas. It also confirms that most voters in the Northeast voted for Lula in the runoff, as did many of the cities in the North along the Amazon River (Santarém being the biggest exception).

The second point comes up when we look at specific regions and try to set aside certain impressions. An interesting example appears when you zoom into the South. The region is always described as very conservative, right-wing, but you can spot countless cities voting for Lula, even in Santa Catarina, a state popularly nicknamed “Bolsonaristan”. When I started drawing the map, I chose to set apart the places where the race was tight, with a margin under 10 percentage points: they appear in lighter shades. Even before I started studying the branch of political science that looks at political behaviour, party movements and so on, I used to think about the many ways people might vote, especially when “unfair” associations are made. As I said about Santa Catarina, it’s natural to think that each neighbourhood or city belongs to one camp or the other. But there are many places where the contest was more balanced, and it’s great to see the mobilisation from one round to the next.

This brings me to the third point about this map. Right after the results came out, we heard that Flávio won in 80% of the militia-controlled areas of Rio de Janeiro. Yes, that’s true. But it’s impossible to ignore the courage of the people who, even under threat, went out to vote and secured a more balanced result in their sections. In most sections along the Campo Grande/Santa Cruz axis, in Rio’s West Zone, the margin was under 20 points. And more importantly: at a quick glance, I couldn’t find a single section in these areas where Flávio’s vote grew more than Lula’s.

The idea of this interactive map is to show that Brazil’s electoral system values every single vote. If Brazil had an Electoral College like the United States, we’d probably be telling a different story. Luckily, that’s not the case. Let’s value every vote cast for the democratic camp!

I’ll post something about abstention soon, too!

Oh, and feel free to check out the other things on the website (not that there’s much there…).

item.title: Coalition support in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies
item.description:
Back to Stories

These charts show how coalition parties in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies voted on executive bills between 2003 and 2018, alongside the positions they held in government.

NoteSource

Aggregated from the replication data for “Bureaucratic appointments and coalition support in presidential systems” (Party Politics, 2026). Only party and coalition totals are shown, and party results based on fewer than five deputies voting are withheld.

The data at a glance

What the replication data contain and how much of it reaches this page.

Support and positions over time

Pick a party and a tier. Shaded columns show the party’s share of posts in that tier for each coalition-year it was a member. Dots show, for each roll call, the share of the party’s voting deputies who followed the president, and the line marks the coalition-year average.

Party
Positions

Share of posts Roll call Coalition-year average Not in the coalition No roll calls in the data

Show as table

Roll calls

Each bar is one roll call on an executive bill, split into the share of deputies voting who followed the president (right) and who did not (left). Choose a party to see its deputies alone, with a tick marking all coalition parties for comparison. Click a dot in the overview to show only that president's roll calls.

Party
Group by
Bill type

Followed the president Did not follow (against or abstained) All coalition parties

Show as table

Support across groups

Each dot is one party on one roll call. Most results sit at or near 100%, so the comparison rests on the average and on how often a party fell below 90%.

Compare by
Average Middle half of results, line at the median Party result on one roll call

“Below 90%” is the share of party results in which fewer than 90% of the party's voting deputies followed the president. Party results with fewer than five deputies voting are left out. Dots and averages are not weighted by party size; the pooled column in the table counts every deputy vote equally. Centrão follows the classification in the replication data. Election timing follows the article's indicator for roll calls held after the first round of national or local elections.

Summary table

Parties compared

Parties stay in the same order, from highest to lowest support for the president, so switching the measure shows how shares of posts and ideological distance line up with support.

Show
Centrão party Other party Range of coalition-year averages (3+ roll calls)

Support is the share of the party's coalition votes that followed the president, with the range of its coalition-year averages over periods with at least three roll calls. Shares of posts are means of the party's year totals across the years it voted as a coalition member, with the lowest and highest year. Distance to the president's party is the article's ideological distance measure, averaged across the party's roll calls, with the range across years.

Show as table

Correlates of support

Simple correlations between each party-year’s support for the president and the variables used in the article. Click a bar to see the party-years behind it.

Comparison

Positive correlation Negative correlation

These are simple correlations across party-years (2016 is split by president), without the party fixed effects and controls used in the article's models, so they can differ from the article's estimates. Variables keep the order of their correlation with support across all party-years, whatever the selection. “Within parties” subtracts each party's own average first, so only changes within parties over time remain; centrão does not vary within parties and drops out. Party-years with fewer than five votes are left out.

Show as table

About the data

Every number on this page is computed from the article’s replication data and published only as party and coalition totals. Roll calls come from CEBRAP and appointments from ENAP. The charts are descriptive: they show associations in the data, without the controls used in the article’s models.
